cases.summary: Long garden-community lease. Entry-purpose list hides a removal right and a repair shutoff; a broad liability limit hides behind 'unless otherwise required by law'.
Eight-unit building. An AS-IS clause removes the repair duty; the deposit deadline sits in a later section; holdover notice is 15 days.
Scanned-looking mid-rise lease (wrapped lines, page headers). Deposit may sit in the operating account, notice counts weekends, a balcony rule bans flags, abandoned-property clause lacks the legend.
Long single-family house lease. Plumbing shift is allowed for a house; 12-hour entry notice, a gag on code complaints, and a water cutoff for unpaid utility bills are not.

findings.title: Limit on landlord liability
findings.problem: The lease tries to release the landlord from liability the law imposes. Florida makes this kind of clause void.

span.quote: Unless otherwise required by law, Owner is not liable to Resident, occupants or guests for any personal injury or for any damage to or loss of personal property, from any cause, including fire, smoke, rain, flood, water leaks, hail, lightning, wind, explosions, theft, or the acts of other residents.

findings.suggestedFix: Delete the clause. Each party remains responsible for its own obligations and liability under law.

findings.title: Utility shutoff
findings.problem: The lease lets the landlord interrupt utilities to make repairs or prevent damage. Florida's statute bars any landlord-caused utility interruption and states no repair exception; temporary repair work is commonly treated differently, so a person should check how this clause is used.

span.quote: (f) to interrupt water or electrical service when needed to complete repairs

findings.suggestedFix: Landlord may temporarily interrupt a utility only as reasonably necessary for repairs or emergencies, with advance notice to Tenant when practical, and will restore service promptly.

findings.title: Removing the tenant's belongings
findings.problem: The lease lets the landlord remove the tenant's belongings without a surrender, abandonment or court eviction. Florida prohibits this.

span.quote: (e) to remove window coverings, decorations or other items that violate the Community Policies

findings.suggestedFix: Landlord may remove Tenant's personal property only after surrender, abandonment, or a lawful eviction.

findings.title: Deposit return deadline
findings.problem: The lease gives the landlord 45 days to return the deposit when there is no claim. Florida requires 15 days or less, so this term is void.

span.quote: Within forty-five (45) days after Tenant vacates, Landlord will return the security deposit, less any amounts Landlord is entitled to deduct, together with an itemized statement of any deductions.

findings.suggestedFix: Landlord will return the deposit when there is no claim within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement.

findings.title: Deposit claim notice deadline
findings.problem: The lease mentions to send written notice of a claim on the deposit, but the terms are unclear: Article XXXI allows an itemized deduction statement within 45 days, while the printed disclosure states claim notice within 30 days; the lease is contradictory.

span.quote: Within forty-five (45) days after Tenant vacates, Landlord will return the security deposit, less any amounts Landlord is entitled to deduct, together with an itemized statement of any deductions.

findings.title: Notice to end a periodic tenancy
findings.problem: For a month-to-month renewal tenancy the lease allows the tenant to give 15 days' notice and the landlord to give 15 days' notice. Florida requires at least 30 days before the end of the period.

span.quote: If Tenant remains in the Unit after the Lease term with Landlord's consent, the tenancy will be month-to-month at the rent then in effect, and either party may end it by giving the other at least fifteen (15) days' written notice.

findings.suggestedFix: Either party may end this month-to-month renewal tenancy by giving written notice at least 30 days before the end of a rental period.

findings.title: Waiver of landlord's maintenance duties
findings.problem: The lease shifts the landlord's code, structural or plumbing duties to the tenant. For a unit that is not a single-family home or duplex, these duties can't be waived.

span.quote: Landlord has no obligation to make repairs, replacements or improvements to the Unit or the building except those Landlord elects to make in its sole discretion.

findings.suggestedFix: Landlord will comply with applicable building, housing, and health codes and keep the structural components and plumbing in good repair as required by s. 83.51(1), Florida Statutes.

findings.title: Notice before entry for repairs
findings.problem: The lease lets the landlord enter for repairs with 12 hours' notice. Florida requires at least 24 hours' notice for repairs (emergencies excepted).

span.quote: Landlord may enter the Home to inspect it, make repairs, or show it to prospective tenants or buyers upon at least twelve (12) hours' notice to Tenant, between 9:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m.

findings.suggestedFix: Except in an emergency, Landlord will give Tenant at least 24 hours' notice before entering to make repairs.

findings.title: Utility shutoff
findings.problem: The lease allows the landlord to shut off or interrupt utilities. Florida prohibits this, even when rent is late.

span.quote: If Tenant does not reimburse those charges when due, Landlord may have water service to the Home discontinued until Tenant pays.

findings.suggestedFix: Delete the clause. Landlord will not interrupt any utility service furnished to Tenant.

findings.title: Retaliation against the tenant
findings.problem: The lease penalizes the tenant (higher rent, fewer services or termination) for protected conduct such as complaining to a code agency. Florida prohibits retaliation.

span.quote: If Tenant reports a condition to a governmental authority before that period ends, Landlord may terminate this Lease on thirty (30) days' notice.
